extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants (principal investigators) and institutional officials involved in appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the sequential rebuttal and formal appeal process for applicants who believe their NIH grant application was handled inappropriately or biasedly during peer review, including required signatures, content, routing, timing, and possible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two sequential opportunities (rebuttals and appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) provide an applicant who feels that some aspect of the handling or peer review of his/her grant application has been inappropriate, biased, or wrong with two sequential opportunities (respectively referred to as 'rebuttals' and 'appeals') to have his/her concerns addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first opportunity is a rebuttal after receipt of the summary statement; the second is a formal appeal if the Council concurs with the initial review. Use rebuttal first; only if the Council declines deferral/rereview may the applicant submit a formal appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal timing and recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: After receipt of the summary statement that documents the results of the initial review of an application's scientific and/or technical merit, the applicant may submit a letter rebutting the review to the program administrator who is responsible for the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That rebuttal letter will usually be made available to the National Advisory Council/Board of the relevant NIH Institute/Center/Division (ICD) for consideration if ICD staff cannot handle the concerns administratively. Council may recommend that the application be deferred and rereviewed if objections have merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal appeal joint signature requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "The PI and the applicant institution, represented by the institutional official authorized to sign applications, must jointly sign an appeal and send it to the NIH Peer Review Appeals Officer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The institutional official's signature indicates that the applicant institution endorses both form and substance of the appeal (ref: NIH Manual Chapter 4518). Appeals lacking the required joint signatures may not be accepted as properly filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal letter content and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal letter must explain fully the reasons for the disagreement and append supporting documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a complete factual and procedural explanation of the alleged flaws in the review process and attach any corroborating materials; incomplete explanations or absent documentation weaken the appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal submission routing
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals must be sent to the NIH Appeals Officer at the Office of the Director, National Institutes of Health (Building 1, Room 328, Bethesda, MD 20892).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specified routing to ensure the appeal is received by the official responsible for handling appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of appeal (limited to peer review process flaws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals cases examine only whether there were any flaws in the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals are not a challenge to the scientific judgment or merits of the reviewers' conclusions; they are limited to procedural or fairness issues in how the review was conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible outcomes of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The most favorable possible outcome for an applicant in an appeal case can only be a decision that the application in question be rereviewed. The other possible outcome is that the review of the application was not substantially flawed and any minor flaws did not affect the recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the review is found not substantially flawed, the original review stands and the application will not be rereviewed. Applicants should weigh that the only corrective action available via appeal is rereview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of the appeal process
rubrics_metrics.description: As the conduct of an appeal case involves several steps of process and review, it may take at least four months (or one review cycle) to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because appeals can consume a full review cycle, applicants should consider whether pursuing an appeal (with its delay) is preferable to revising and resubmitting the application in a new cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of substantive effect before appealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may wish to consider whether deficiencies in the review of his/her application were substantive enough to have had a major deleterious effect on the review of the application and, if not, to revise and resubmit the application instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only deficiencies that materially affected the review outcome are likely to justify the time and resources of an appeal; minor or inconsequential issues are unlikely to result in rereview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review administrative issues handled separately by DRG/ICD
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant concerns about the acceptance for review, responsiveness to a Request for Applications, other receipt issues, or the referral of their application, when submitted prior to the initial review, are entirely the responsibility of the Division of Research Grants (DRG) or of the ICD assigned to review the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These administrative/receipt/referral matters are actions external to the peer review process and are handled through the DRG or ICD processes, which also provide two opportunities for applicant concerns to be addressed prior to initial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding decisions not appealable
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions regarding the funding of applications may not be appealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because funding decisions are actions external to the peer review process, they fall outside the scope of the appeal mechanism described here.
